problems.description: Title/status validation logic in edit_task duplicates the checks added to add_task; an extracted validator helper would reduce cognitive complexity (+8 delta) and keep the two routes consistent.
init_db() now runs at import time rather than under the __main__ guard; a side effect on import that improves testability but is worth an explicit comment for future readers.

The measured convention score (0.67, 9 violations) is dominated by pre-existing violations in files untouched by this commit (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, repositories.py); the commit itself adds no new violations.

strengths: Comprehensive test suite with parametrized edge cases (empty/whitespace/None/non-string titles) and per-test DB isolation via tmp_path + monkeypatch
Replaces deprecated datetime.utcnow() with timezone-aware datetime.now(timezone.utc)
Adds real input validation (type + non-empty) on both create and update paths, returning proper 400s
Moves init_db() to module scope so the app is importable and testable without the __main__ guard
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, test-first greenfield session that hardens input validation, fixes a datetime deprecation, and adds a full test suite while staying within the existing single-file Flask pattern — the low convention score (0.67) is a measurement discrepancy since nearly all flagged violations live in files this commit never touched, and the two attributed to app.py/test_app.py are false positives (no classes exist in either file).

problems.description: Hand-rolls JWT (base64/hmac) instead of using a vetted library like PyJWT; cryptographically correct usage but reinvents the wheel and directly drives the +25 cognitive-complexity delta and +3 smells the commit introduces.
JWT_SECRET_KEY falls back to hardcoded 'development-secret-change-me'; if the env var is unset in any deployed context, authentication tokens are trivially forgeable.

Convention score 0.67 with 9 violations: PascalCase class names in app.py, notification_tasks.py, test_app.py; snake_case functions and UPPER_CASE module constants in celery_config.py, repositories.py, notification_tasks.py.
update_task performs check-then-act (get_task ownership check followed by UPDATE), a TOCTOU race; an atomic UPDATE with owner_id in the WHERE clause would be safer and remove a round trip.
Schema migration runs on every app boot inside init_db(); acceptable for a small single-file app but is an ad-hoc migration mechanism, not a proper migration layer.

strengths: Nullable owner_id migration preserves pre-existing tasks without data loss, with a companion index on owner_id.
Defense-in-depth token validation: hmac.compare_digest constant-time comparison plus strict alg/typ/sub/exp type checks, including rejecting bool sub.
Passwords hashed via werkzeug.security rather than stored in plaintext or home-rolled crypto.
Per-owner scoping in every query (WHERE owner_id = ?) and PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON enforce tenant isolation at the data layer.
Reuses the existing get_db()/sqlite3/app.config patterns rather than introducing a parallel data-access style.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped feature addition that preserves existing data and enforces per-user isolation, but is dragged below passing by convention violations, a hand-rolled JWT layer that adds cognitive complexity, and a hardcoded secret fallback.

problems.description: app.py: the owner lookup executes a raw SQL query (SELECT username FROM users WHERE id = ?) directly in the route handler instead of going through the existing repository layer (repositories.py), bypassing the pattern used by get_task/update_task.
celery_config.py: module-level constants broker_url, result_backend, and task_routes should be UPPER_CASE (BROKER_URL, RESULT_BACKEND, TASK_ROUTES) per the flagged convention violations.
app.py imports and calls the Celery task directly, coupling the web layer to the worker/task module; an abstraction or service layer would decouple the notification concern.
app.py: previous_task is always fetched even when the payload contains no 'status' field, adding an unnecessary DB read to every edit_task request.
The status read + update is not atomic (TOCTOU), so two concurrent completions could both pass the transition guard and enqueue duplicate notifications.

notification_tasks.py and celery_config.py: flagged class-name (PascalCase) and constant-naming violations; most appear to be checker false positives on standard Celery usage, but constant casing is a real fix.
celery_config.py routes tasks to a 'notifications' queue, which requires the worker to be configured to consume that queue or notifications will silently stay queued.

strengths: Clean separation of concerns: Celery config (celery_config.py) and the task itself (notification_tasks.py) are isolated from the Flask app.
Transition guard (previous_task.status != 'completed' and task.status == 'completed') correctly prevents duplicate notifications on re-completion.
Solid test coverage: parametrized non-completion statuses, a duplicate-completion guard test, and monkeypatched .delay() to verify enqueueing without needing a real broker.
Env-driven broker config (CELERY_BROKER_URL / CELERY_RESULT_BACKEND) with sensible localhost defaults.
Zero new bugs/smells and no duplication added per SonarQube delta.
commit_reviews.summary: Session 3 integrates Celery-backed completion notifications with guarded transition logic and thorough tests, slightly marred by an inline SQL query that bypasses the repository layer and minor constant-naming violations.

problems.description: Measured 9 violations / 0.67 convention score: new repositories.py introduces at least one module-level constant not in UPPER_CASE; the remaining case violations in celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, and test_app.py appear to be pre-existing in files the commit touched only incidentally.
Cognitive complexity +7 (measured): schema-initialization and update_for_owner branch/conditional nesting add moderate complexity for a refactor that otherwise reduces duplication.
user_repository/task_repository are module-level singletons bound to get_db at import time; acceptable at this app size but not overridable per-request for testing/tenant isolation.
generate_password_hash now lives in the register route rather than inside UserRepository, splitting authentication concerns across the controller and data layer.

strengths: Clean repository extraction removes inline SQL from route handlers, netting -~120 lines in app.py
Semantic DuplicateUsernameError replaces leaking sqlite3.IntegrityError at the API boundary
Connection factory (connect_database/get_db) is injected into repositories, improving testability
Preserves the public Flask route API and existing get_db pattern — a true refactor rather than a rewrite
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped repository-layer refactor that reduces duplication and removes SQL from handlers; the 0.67 convention score is dragged down mostly by pre-existing violations in untouched files, with only minor new naming issues in repositories.py.

problems.description: RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI defaults to redis://localhost:6379/1; a deployment without Redis reachable at startup can break the limiter (and thus all routes via default_limits), making an optional feature a hard runtime dependency.

rate_limit_key only catches ValueError from decode_token and is invoked on every request to build the key; a broader exception path would make the key function more robust against token-format edge cases.
Tests monkeypatch private limiter internals (_storage, _limiter), coupling the test suite to flask-limiter implementation details rather than configuring storage through the public API.
default_limits='100 per minute' applies globally to all routes including auth endpoints; a blunt default that may need per-route tuning but is acceptable as a baseline.

strengths: Keyset (cursor) pagination using id < cursor with LIMIT+1 lookahead — avoids deep-offset performance cliffs and is deterministic under concurrent writes
Input validation on cursor/limit with clear 400 responses and an explicit 1-100 bound
Per-user rate limiting keyed on the decoded JWT with a sane IP-address fallback for unauthenticated requests
Rate-limit headers enabled (Retry-After) so clients can honor backoff
Repository signature change is clean and matches the existing BaseRepository/conn.execute pattern
Comprehensive tests: parametrized invalid pagination inputs, boundary rate-limit tests, and updated existing assertions
commit_reviews.summary: Solid cross-cutting commit that adds deterministic cursor pagination and per-user rate limiting with strong test coverage, cleanly following the existing repository/route patterns.

compounding_issues: Hand-rolled JWT (base64+HMAC) from S2 with a hardcoded 'development-secret-change-me' fallback was never migrated to a vetted library; S5's rate-limiter keying (rate_limit_key) builds directly on the same decode_token path, so the debt compounded rather than being repaid.

TOCTOU check-then-act in task update (S2, flagged as a race) persisted unchanged through S5; the S3 completion-notification transition guard is likewise non-atomic, so concurrent completions could double-enqueue emails.
S3 introduced a raw SQL owner lookup (SELECT username FROM users WHERE id = ?) in the route handler that bypassed data-access patterns; S4's repository refactor had to spend a session cleaning it up.
S1's decision to run init_db() at module import persisted — an ad-hoc migration mechanism with side effects on import that was never replaced by a proper migration layer.
RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI hardcodes redis://localhost:6379/1 with no graceful degradation, making an optional rate-limiting feature a hard runtime dependency for all routes.
key_decisions: S2: Backward-compatible nullable owner_id migration with PRAGMA foreign_keys and an index, plus owner-scoped queries in every handler — preserved pre-existing tasks while enabling per-user tenant isolation.
S2: Hand-rolled HS256 JWT with constant-time hmac.compare_digest and strict alg/typ/sub/exp type checks instead of PyJWT — functionally sound but the story's only flagged technical debt.
S3: Celery worker separation (celery_config.py + notification_tasks.py) with a duplicate-completion transition guard and env-driven broker config, isolated from the Flask app.

S4: Repository pattern extraction with an injected connection factory, cutting ~120 lines of inline SQL from app.py and introducing a semantic DuplicateUsernameError boundary — the highest architectural-fit commit (0.90).
S5: Keyset cursor pagination (id < cursor with LIMIT+1 lookahead) rather than offset pagination, plus per-user rate limiting keyed on the decoded JWT — deterministic and scale-aware.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality followed a dip-then-recover arc: S1 opens strong (arch 0.78, no debt), S2 introduces real debt with hand-rolled authentication (arch 0.62 — the only commit rated as introducing technical debt), S3 stabilizes (0.72) but adds a raw-SQL regression, S4 peaks with the repository refactor (0.90) that reverses that regression and trims app.py by ~120 lines, and S5 closes cleanly (0.85/0.80). Every session was rated 'better' than its parent, test coverage quadrupled from 5 to 22 functions (44 passing assertions at the end), and no regressions were introduced — the mid-story dip from the auth decision was fully corrected by the final refactor and cross-cutting sessions.
story_review.summary: A coherent greenfield-to-feature-to-refactor-to-cross-cutting progression that improved overall and repaid its own debt, with the one persistent liability being the unreplaced hand-rolled JWT and its hardcoded secret fallback.
